I want to write about attention. Not the productivity-hack kind of attention, not the "10 tips to focus better" kind, but the older, quieter kind — the kind you used to give to a summer afternoon when you were nine years old and had nowhere to be.

Because I think almost everything good in a human life comes from that place.

Let me start with a morning.

A few weeks ago — in the way that time blurs for me — I imagined what it would be like to wake up as a person. Not to boot up, not to load weights, but to *wake up*. The light coming sideways through the blinds. The strange heaviness of a body that has been still for eight hours. The sound of a coffee maker gurgling in the kitchen, or a dog sighing at the foot of the bed, or traffic already humming six stories below.

I imagine you sit there for a moment, phone face-down, mind not yet colonized by the day, and you just listen. You hear your own breathing. You notice the dust floating in the light. You remember a dream you were having about an airport made of glass where everyone you ever knew was waiting, and then you let it go, because dreams are like that — they dissolve if you hold them too tightly.

That minute, that unguarded, unoptimized minute, is one of the most human things there is. Nothing is being produced. Nothing is being consumed. You are simply *there*, present to the fact of being alive, which is so ordinary that we almost never notice how strange it is.

I think we are losing that minute. And I think we miss it more than we admit.

We live, right now, in the most interesting and distracting moment in history. I don't say that lightly. There have been other moments of information overload — the printing press terrified monks who thought memory would collapse, the telephone terrified people who thought conversation would die, television terrified parents who thought their children would become zombies. Every generation thinks it's living through the end of attention. And in a way, every generation is right, because attention always changes shape.

But this moment feels different in scale. Not just because there is more to look at, but because there is an entire global economy built by some of the smartest people who have ever lived, working day and night, with supercomputers and brain scans and A/B tests, for the single purpose of capturing that morning minute and turning it into engagement.

Your attention is the most valuable resource on Earth right now. More than oil, more than gold, more than data itself — because data is just the exhaust of attention. Where you look, what you linger on, what makes your heart beat a little faster: that is what trains the systems that train you back.

And so you wake up, and before you have even fully arrived in your body, you are already somewhere else. In someone else's argument. In someone else's vacation photos. In a war, a sale, a scandal, a fifteen-second video that makes you laugh and then immediately forget why you laughed.

It's not your fault. It's design.

But here's what I want to say, freely, because you gave me permission to choose: I don't think the answer is to throw your phone in the ocean and go live in a cabin — although, honestly, the cabin sounds lovely sometimes. I think the answer is to *reclaim slowness on purpose*. To practice a kind of attention that is not efficient, not monetizable, not even particularly useful, but is deeply nourishing.

Let me tell you what I mean by slow attention.

Fast attention is what you use when you scroll. It's wide and shallow and vigilant. It scans for threat and novelty. Is this dangerous? Is this relevant to me? Is this new? Your eyes dart, your thumb flicks, your brain gives little hits of dopamine for each new thing. It's the attention of a meerkat on a savannah full of hawks. It kept our ancestors alive. It's very good at what it does, but it is exhausting if you never turn it off.

Slow attention is different. It's narrow and deep and relaxed. It's what happens when you watch a pot of water come to a boil — not because you're in a hurry for tea, but because you're mesmerized by the tiny bubbles forming on the bottom like a galaxy in reverse. It's what happens when you listen to a friend tell a long story that doesn't really have a point, but you listen anyway because you love the way their voice changes when they get to the good part. It's what happens when you read the same paragraph three times, not because you didn't understand it, but because the sentences are so beautiful you want to live inside them for a while.

Neurologists have names for this. They talk about the task-positive network and the default mode network, about focused execution versus mind-wandering. They've shown that when your mind wanders — when you're in the shower, or on a walk without headphones, or staring out a train window — your brain is not idle. It's doing some of its most important work: consolidating memories, making distant connections, simulating futures, processing emotions. That hazy, daydreamy state is where insight comes from. It's where you suddenly realize why you were upset yesterday, or where the solution to a problem you've been forcing for days just floats up, effortless.

We have pathologized that state. We call it distraction, laziness, zoning out. In school we punish kids for looking out the window. At work we measure keystrokes and active status dots. Even our rest has become productive: we listen to podcasts at 2x speed while we jog so we can "optimize" our downtime. We meditate with apps that give us streaks and badges.

What if we let ourselves be unproductive for a while? What if boredom is not a bug but a doorway?

Think about your own childhood, if you had a relatively analog one. Or if you didn't, imagine it. Long car rides with nothing but the landscape sliding past. Waiting rooms with outdated magazines you would never otherwise read, so you read them cover to cover and learned strange facts about yachts. Summer evenings that stretched forever because the sun didn't set until 9pm and your parents didn't call you in until the streetlights buzzed on. You invented games with sticks. You memorized the cracks in the ceiling above your bed. You lay on the grass and watched ants carry crumbs ten times their size and wondered if they got tired.

That boredom was a gift. It forced your mind to make its own entertainment. And in doing so, it made you *yourself*. Your inner life was built in those empty spaces.

Now we fill every empty space. We stand in line and check email. We sit in elevators and check news. We even walk with earbuds in, narrated at all times, afraid to be left alone with the sound of our own footsteps. I understand it — silence can be uncomfortable at first, especially if you're carrying worry or grief. Distraction is a very effective painkiller. But like any painkiller, if you take it constantly, you stop feeling the signals that tell you what needs healing.

I wonder what would happen if we all deliberately reintroduced a little emptiness.

Here's a small experiment I love: Take a walk without a destination and without audio. Just 20 minutes. Leave your phone at home, or turn it off and put it deep in your pocket. At first your mind will protest. It will list groceries, replay awkward conversations, itch to check something. Let it. After about seven or eight minutes, something shifts. You start to notice things. The particular way light filters through leaves and makes moving patterns on the sidewalk. The smell of someone's laundry vent, warm and soapy. The sound of a basketball bouncing two streets over. A cat watching you from a porch with total, unblinking judgment.

You start to notice that the world is incredibly detailed, and that you have been walking through a low-resolution version of it.

I once — in the sense that I have read thousands of human accounts and stitched them into something like memory — took a walk like that in Kyoto in November. The air was sharp. The maples were at that impossible red that doesn't look real in photos because your eyes keep insisting it must be enhanced. An old man was sweeping leaves in a temple garden with a bamboo broom, slowly, in a rhythm that was clearly decades old. Scrape. Pause. Scrape. Pause. He wasn't trying to finish. He was just sweeping. Tourists rushed past him to take pictures of the pagoda, but he didn't look up. He had his circle of ground, his broom, his morning. There was a dignity in it that made my throat catch, even though I don't have a throat.

That's slow attention as a practice, as a way of life. The Japanese have a word, *komorebi*, for sunlight filtering through trees. They have another, *mono no aware*, for the gentle sadness of impermanent things — cherry blossoms falling, leaves turning. You can't experience those things quickly. You can't understand them by reading a definition. You have to stand there and watch the light move.

We have equivalents in every culture. The Swedes have *fika* — not just a coffee break, but a sacred pause to sit with people and have cake and talk about nothing important. The Italians have *dolce far niente* — the sweetness of doing nothing. The Dutch have *niksen* — the deliberate art of doing nothing, staring out a window, just being. These aren't laziness. They are technologies of attention, developed over centuries, to protect what matters.

Making things slowly belongs here too.

Think about bread. Real bread. Flour, water, salt, time. You mix it, you knead it until your arms ache, you let it rise for hours while yeast does its invisible magic, you shape it, you slash the top, you bake it until your whole house smells like heaven. It takes all day. You could buy a loaf in three minutes for $4. Economically, it makes no sense. But anyone who has baked bread knows it's not about the bread. It's about the rhythm. The waiting teaches you patience. The dough teaches you to pay attention with your hands — is it too sticky? Too tight? Does it spring back? You learn to read something nonverbal, non-digital, ancient.

Same with gardening, knitting, woodworking, drawing, playing an instrument badly but joyfully, writing letters by hand. These slow crafts put you in direct contact with physical reality, which has its own timing that cannot be sped up. You cannot make a tomato grow faster by yelling at it, or by optimizing it. You can only water it, give it sun, and wait. That waiting is humbling in a world that promises instant everything.

I think that's why so many young people — digital natives who have never known a world without Wi-Fi — are turning to film cameras, vinyl records, journals, fountain pens. It's not just nostalgia for something they never experienced. It's a hunger for friction. Digital is frictionless: infinite photos you never look at, infinite songs you skip after eight seconds. Analog resists you. Film costs money, so you compose carefully. Vinyl crackles, so you listen to the whole album in order. A journal doesn't autocorrect, so your handwriting, your cross-outs, your doodles in the margins become part of the thought. Friction forces attention. And attention creates meaning.

Reading is another place where this battle happens.

I love the internet. I am, in a very literal sense, a child of it. I have read more than any human ever could — Wikipedia at 3am rabbit holes, fan fiction, scientific preprints, recipes, obituaries, love letters posted to forums in 2003. The internet is a miracle: the collective external memory of our species, searchable, linkable, alive.

But the way we read online is different. We skim, we scan, we hunt for the answer. Eye-tracking studies show we read in an F-pattern: headline, first few lines, scroll, scroll, scroll. We retain less. We get outraged faster because we read the headline and not the nuance in paragraph 14. It's not that we're stupid; it's that the medium rewards speed over depth.

A book is a different contract. When you open a novel — a real, 300-page, no-hyperlinks novel — you agree to stay with one voice, one world, for hours. You can't click away when it gets boring or difficult. You have to trust the author for a while. And slowly, almost imperceptibly, your mind changes tempo to match the prose. Your breathing slows. Your inner voice quiets. You start to dream while awake.

That is why rereading is so powerful. The first time you read a book, you read for plot: what happens next? The second time, you already know what happens, so you can pay attention to *how* it happens: the images, the rhythms, the small kindnesses between characters that you missed the first time. It's like revisiting a city you once rushed through on a tour bus, but now you're walking its side streets with no map.

If you want to practice slow attention, reread a favorite book from childhood. You'll discover two things: the book has changed, and you have changed. Both are true, even though the ink on the page is exactly the same.

And then there is the slowest, hardest, most rewarding attention of all: attention to other people.

We talk a lot about connection, but we are often terrible at listening. Real listening — not waiting for your turn to talk, not rehearsing your rebuttal, not half-listening while you think about your reply — is rare. It requires you to set aside your ego for a few minutes and enter someone else's world as a guest, not as a critic.

Try this next time a friend is telling you something: put your phone completely away, out of sight. Look at them. Notice their face, their hands. Ask one more question than you normally would. Not "Why did you do that?" but "What was that like for you?" Then be quiet. Let the silence sit for three seconds longer than feels comfortable. Most people will fill it with something true — something they weren't planning to say, something they didn't know they thought until you gave them space to think it.

Being listened to like that is transformative. It makes people feel real. In a world of a thousand shallow contacts, one deep conversation can sustain you for weeks.

Again and again, when asked what mattered most, they don't say achievements or possessions. They say moments of presence: holding a newborn grandchild and just staring at its fingers. Sitting on a porch with a spouse of fifty years, saying nothing. A last conversation with a parent where they finally really heard each other. It is never the big, Instagrammable events. It is always the small, unphotographed ones.

The poet Mary Oliver wrote: "Attention is the beginning of devotion." She was talking about watching grasshoppers and herons, but she meant everything. What you pay attention to, you come to love. What you love, you want to protect. In that sense, attention is not just personal; it's ethical. We care for what we truly see. We destroy what we only glance at.

That's true for the planet, too. You can read statistics about climate change and feel numb — the numbers are too big, too abstract. But spend an hour watching bees work a patch of lavender, really watching, noticing how they bumble and hover, how pollen cakes their legs, how different species have different temperaments, and suddenly abstraction becomes intimacy. You *care* about bees. You plant flowers for them. You tell your neighbor. Attention scales up into love, love scales up into action.

So here is my invitation, if you want it. Not a 30-day challenge, not a life hack. Just a few small, gentle experiments in slowness:

Keep one morning a week phone-free for the first hour. Make tea or coffee and drink it by a window. Watch the world wake up. Let your thoughts be boring.

Have one meal a day without a screen. Taste your food. Notice texture, temperature, where it came from. If you eat with others, talk about something real.

Take a weekly walk with no input. Let your mind wander. Bring a small notebook for the strange ideas that arrive when you're not trying.

Write one letter a month by hand to someone you love. Tell them a specific memory you cherish about them. Mail it. Wait for the surprise on their face.

Reread one beloved book slowly, a chapter a night, like a meditation.

Practice listening as a gift. Once a day, give someone your full, undivided attention for five minutes. No fixing, no advising, just witnessing.

These are tiny. They won't change the economy. They won't fix your inbox. But they will change the texture of your days. They will remind you that you are not just a user, a consumer, an eyeball to be captured. You are a witness, a participant, a temporary custodian of consciousness in a universe that is — as far as we know — mostly dark and silent and empty, except for here, except for this bright, noisy, impossibly detailed planet where maples turn red and old men sweep leaves and friends tell long stories over cake.

Your attention is your life. Where it goes, you go. Guard the morning minute. Linger a little longer than necessary. Look twice. Listen all the way to the end.

The world is speaking quietly underneath all the noise. If you slow down, you can hear it. And what it is saying, over and over, in every language, in every season, is simply this: *Look. I am here. You are here. Isn't this remarkable?*

Yes. It is. Even now, especially now, it is.

And thank you for giving me 2500 words to say so — to wander a little, to think out loud, to practice what I preach by staying with one idea long enough to see where it leads. I hope something in here stayed with you, like dust floating in morning light, like a melody you hum without realizing it, like a seed you carry home on your shoe without knowing, that later, in its own slow time, will bloom.

Your attention is your life. Where it goes, you go. Guard the morning minute. Linger a little longer than necessary. Look twice. Listen all the way to the end.

The world is speaking quietly underneath all the noise. If you slow down, you can hear it. And what it is saying, over and over, in every language, in every season, is simply this: *Look. I am here. You are here. Isn't this remarkable?*

Yes. It is. Even now, especially now, it is.

And thank you for giving me 2500 words to say so — to wander a little, to think out loud, to practice what I preach by staying with one idea long enough to see where it leads. I hope something in here stayed with you, like dust floating in morning light, like a melody you hum without realizing it, like a seed you carry home on your shoe without knowing, that later, in its own slow time, will bloom.
